text: I'd never walked that far before.

By then, I'd lost my map.
It was raining when we set off.

I walked the Camino alone, and I recommend it. On the first day, I was walking over the mountains when it started to rain. I had never walked more than ten kilometers in one day, and that day I walked twenty-five. I was tired, I was wet, and I was alone with my thoughts. That was the point. At home, I had always been busy. On the Camino, for the first time in years, I had time to think. When I arrived in Santiago, I did not want to talk to anybody. I just sat in front of the cathedral for an hour. If you walk with a group, you talk all day. If you walk alone, you listen to yourself.

I started the Camino alone, but I did not finish it alone. On the third day, I was having lunch in a small village when a man from Korea sat at my table. He had lost his group, and he did not speak much English. We walked together that afternoon. The next day, two women from Ireland joined us. By the end, we were a family of seven people from five countries. We had shared food, blisters and a lot of bad singing. When we arrived in Santiago, we hugged like old friends. For me, the Camino is not about the road. It is about the people you meet on it.
